item.title: “Monks, there are these three unwholesome thoughts: sensual thought, ill-will thought, harmful thought. And these three unwholesome thoughts are abandoned without remainder in one whose…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these three unwholesome thoughts: sensual thought, ill-will thought, harmful thought. And these three unwholesome thoughts are abandoned without remainder in one whose mind is well established in the four foundations of mindfulness or who develops the signless concentration. Monks, develop the signless concentration well. When the signless concentration is developed and cultivated, it brings great fruit and great benefit.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.80
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: The eye is unguarded, The faculties are unrestrained — Flies will swarm Thoughts of craving. The monk becomes rotten, Filled with foul smells — Far,…
item.description:
The eye is unguarded,
The faculties are unrestrained —
Flies will swarm
Thoughts of craving.
The monk becomes rotten,
Filled with foul smells —
Far, far away is Nibbāna!
He meets with misfortune.
In village or forest,
If one’s self is not peaceful,
The fool, without wisdom,
Walking or standing, is full of flies.
But one endowed with virtue,
Delighting in tranquil wisdom,
Lives peacefully and happily —
All flies are destroyed.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.128
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Furthermore, monks, one might see that woman — sick, suffering, gravely ill, lying in her own urine and feces, needing others to lift her, needing…
item.description:
“Furthermore, monks, one might see that woman — sick, suffering, gravely ill, lying in her own urine and feces, needing others to lift her, needing others to lay her down. What do you think, monks? Has her former charm and beauty disappeared and peril become evident?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Thus, monks, is the peril in the case of forms.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 13 – Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands that it is impermanent, he understands that it is not to be clung to, he understands that…
item.description:
“If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands that it is impermanent, he understands that it is not to be clung to, he understands that it is not to be delighted in. If he feels a painful feeling … If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands that it is impermanent, he understands that it is not to be clung to, he understands that it is not to be delighted in. If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it with a mind free from attachment. If he feels a painful feeling … If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it with a mind free from attachment.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.51
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “When ignorance leads the way, monks, for the attainment of unwholesome states, then lack of conscience and lack of fear of wrongdoing follow. For one…
item.description:
“When ignorance leads the way, monks, for the attainment of unwholesome states, then lack of conscience and lack of fear of wrongdoing follow. For one overwhelmed by ignorance and without wisdom, monks, wrong view arises. For one with wrong view, wrong intention arises. For one with wrong intention, wrong speech arises. For one with wrong speech, wrong action arises. For one with wrong action, wrong livelihood arises. For one with wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises. For one with wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises. For one with wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises.

When true knowledge leads the way, monks, for the attainment of wholesome states, then conscience and fear of wrongdoing follow. For one with true knowledge and wisdom, monks, right view arises. For one with right view, right intention arises. For one with right intention, right speech arises. For one with right speech, right action arises. For one with right action, right livelihood arises. For one with right livelihood, right effort arises. For one with right effort, right mindfulness arises. For one with right mindfulness, right concentration arises.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.1
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: The five aggregates are the burden, The bearer of the burden is the person. Taking up the burden is suffering in the world, Laying down…
item.description:
The five aggregates are the burden,
The bearer of the burden is the person.
Taking up the burden is suffering in the world,
Laying down the burden is happiness, free from suffering.
Having laid down the heavy burden,
One takes up no other burden.
Having pulled out craving, root and all,
One is free from hunger and thirst,
Fully extinguished, at peace.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.22
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, one who does not directly know and fully understand everything, not having his mind dispassionate toward it, abandoning it, cannot make an end of…
item.description:
“Monks, one who does not directly know and fully understand everything, not having his mind dispassionate toward it, abandoning it, cannot make an end of suffering. One who directly knows and fully understands everything, having his mind dispassionate toward it, abandoning it, can make an end of suffering.” The Blessed One spoke this meaning. Here it is said:

One who knows and understands
Everything as everything,
And does not lust for anything anywhere —
Such a one, indeed,
Has fully understood everything
And can pass beyond
All suffering.

From: Itivuttaka 7
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, those ascetics or brahmins in the past … in the future … in the present who regard whatever in the world is agreeable and…
item.description:
“Monks, those ascetics or brahmins in the past … in the future … in the present who regard whatever in the world is agreeable and enticing as impermanent, as suffering, as not-self, as a disease, as fearful — they abandon craving. Those who abandon craving, abandon attachment. Those who abandon attachment, abandon suffering. Those who abandon suffering are freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that they are freed from suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.66
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, I am freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, you too are freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, wander…
item.description:
“Monks, I am freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, you too are freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, wander for the happiness of the many, for the welfare of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, happiness, and welfare of gods and humans. Do not go two by the same road. Monks, teach the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing. Proclaim the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. There are beings with little dust in their eyes who, if they do not hear the Dhamma, will decline. They will become those who understand the Dhamma. Monks, I will go to Uruvelā, the town of Senā, to teach the Dhamma.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.5
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “But this body, Aggivessana, is material, composed of the four great elements, born of father and mother, nourished with rice and porridge, impermanent, subject to…
item.description:
“But this body, Aggivessana, is material, composed of the four great elements, born of father and mother, nourished with rice and porridge, impermanent, subject to rubbing, pressing, breaking, disintegration, dissolution. It should be contemplated as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, as not-self. When he contemplates this body as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease … as not-self, then bodily desire, bodily fondness, bodily subjection are abandoned.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 74 – Dīghanakhasutta
📖 Read this sutta
